correctness.rationale: The actual source defines the Minkowski relative gauge with difference body D=(C−C)/2 and prescribes a pentagon vertex, NOT globally optimized first boundary point. An independent exact Q(√5) calculation reconstructed all five pentagon vertices and all ten D vertices, checked D is precisely the convex hull of all 25 pairwise half-differences, proved all six successive cyclic edge vectors have Minkowski gauge d=3(√5−1)/4, checked exact parameter ordering and d/(2+d)=3−6√5/5. The independent construction establishes existence. Lassak 2004 Theorem 1 and immediately following observation (materially read in primary full text) prove every relatively equilateral k≥4 polygon through the same boundary vertex has the same side length, establishing universality. Dihedral symmetry and affine invariance extend to all vertices and affine pentagon images. No global optimum d_C(6) is claimed.
residual_risks: The universal same-vertex uniqueness theorem is a cited primary published lemma, not rederived from the exact algebra alone.
The computation does not prove global d_C(6), worst-body six-copy conjectures or higher-dimensional extensions.

evidence: Lassak 2004 Theorem 1 and the subsequent observation prove existence and equal side lengths for all same-prescribed-vertex relative equilateral k-gons when k≥4; this structural universal theorem does NOT determine the actual value for a regular pentagon.

Böröczky–Lángi 2005, also Lángi dissertation six-point chapter, establishes optimal six ARBITRARY points with pentagon five vertices and its interior center at distance 2−2√5/5. Boundary-inscribed six-point equilateral hexagon and vertex anchor are excluded by that equality configuration.
Lángi 2003 gives general convex-hexagon relative-length bounds; Lángi–Lassak 2003 gives a general packing conversion and a distinct three-copy pentagon example.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Neither stronger-sounding six-arbitrary-points theorem nor universal existence and general bounds logically force the claimed exact vertex-anchored d_v. They differ in boundary requirement, quantifier or omitted explicit value.

value.rationale: The fixed pentagon vertex is canonically determined rather than an arbitrary numerical slice: Lassak’s k≥4 theorem guarantees a single common side length for every equilateral hexagon sharing it. The regular pentagon is singled out in the source literature as a likely extremal geometry for six homothetic copies, but its illustrated numerical benchmark is only approximately 0.32. The exact algebraic anchored value and homothetic ratio form a natural, exact, reproducible geometric invariant with potential use in testing or bounding unresolved global packing problems. A finite exact natural classification need not settle the global conjecture.
residual_risks: The closed form is only vertex-anchored, not the best arrangement among all boundary points or all bodies.
Earlier unknown computations behind the numerical diagram may affect historical novelty and perceived value.

final_claim: Let C be a regular pentagon or any invertible affine image, D=(C−C)/2 its relative Minkowski unit ball and v any pentagon vertex. Every C-relative equilateral inscribed six-gon containing v has common relative side length 3(√5−1)/4. The corresponding six-positive-homothet ratio from r=d/(2+d) is 3−6√5/5. This does NOT determine the free-first-point/global six-point boundary value d_C(6) or the worst-body packing problem.
limitations: No global d_C(6) or worst-body theorem.
